In parts of the world, the collection of available fuel such as firewood, dung cake, and agricultural waste for home use can take 200-300 person-days per year.  As well as being time-consuming, the typical patterns of collection lead to deforestation, soil erosion, and ecological imbalances.  In the future, experts predict that even if food supplies are adequate for rural populations, fuel supplies for domestic consumption may not be.

In light of such considerations, aid organizations in parts of Asia and Africa have developed solar ovens for use in rural societies. Such ovens are cheaply constructed, easily operated, and extremely energy efficient. The device usually consists of an inner and outer metal or cardboard box, a top cover, and two panes of plain glass. The inner box is painted black to absorb maximum solar radiation. The space between the two boxes is filled with an insulating material such as rice husks, which are easily available and which, because of their high silicon content, neither attract insects nor rot easily. Other easily available materials for insulation are ground nutshells, coconut shells, or newspaper. An adjustable mirror mounted on one side of the oven box reflects the sunlight into the interior, boosting the temperatures by 15 to 30 degrees Celsius. This boost is most useful during the winter, when the sun is lower. Inside the oven, a temperature between 80 degrees and 120 degrees Celsius above the ambient temperature can be maintained. Such a temperature is sufficient to cook food gradually but completely. Trials have shown that all typical food dishes can be prepared in this solar device without loss of taste or nutrition.

Apart from being cheap and efficient, preparing food in solar ovens offers several welcome advantages over traditional cooking methods. Traditional indoor wood fires produce choking smoke that causes respiratory and eye diseases. They are also a fire hazard, especially for small children. Finally, the combustion of wood and other biofuels produces carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases that contribute to global warming. % For all these reasons, solar cooking is beginning to make a significant improvement in the lives of millions of families in rural societies.

Until recently, some abnormal growth conditions in humans were treated with the growth hormone, which is produced in the pituitary gland in the brain. This substance was used to treat children whose own pituitary glands did not produce enough growth hormone because of, for example, a tumor in the gland, or perhaps because of trauma. The resulting condition, pituitary dwarfism, meant that the individual would attain a small overall stature by adulthood. The natural cadaver-derived growth hormone was taken off the market after it was linked to a brain disease that attacked some of the children undergoing treatment.

A replacement for the abandoned treatment is a new synthetic growth hormone that, it is claimed, has fewer severe side effects and can be produced in unlimited quantities. This drug, Somatrem, is produced by genetic engineering and has been demonstrated to be equivalent to natural human growth hormone. Among the drug's effects are the stimulation of skeletal growth and the ability to increase the number and size of muscle cells.

For children who are deficient in their own growth hormone, the development of Somatrem has been an important medical advance.  The problem is that the drug may be abused by people who produce an adequate output of the substance and are, therefore, not medically in need of its benefits. For example, athletes may take the drug in the belief that it will improve their physique and physical performance because of its suggested anabolic properties. Recently, other medical preparations incorporating the drug have been touted as an anti-aging formula.

It has been found, however, that the unsupervised use of this drug may create medical problems including severe headaches, the creation of a diabetic condition in the body, and abnormal growth of bones and body organs. For such reasons, some experts have recommended that registers be kept of legitimate Somatrem recipients. The implications of the use of Somatrem must be thoroughly understood before widespread distribution of the drug is undertaken.

Many researchers believe that apes can communicate with human beings. Investigations made at laboratories in the United States and elsewhere indicate that chimpanzees and gorillas are capable of understanding language and using linguistic responses at the level of a four-year-old child. Washoe, an adult chimpanzee who was raised as if she were a deaf child, can translate words she hears into American Sign Language. Koko, a 400-pound lowland gorilla, is claimed to have understood a poem written about her. Tests of Koko's auditory co between many sounds.

The investigators at the forefront of this research admit that their work has been severely criticized. For behavior to be called "language," it must be communicative; in other words, the signer mumust be able to use language creatively. He or she should be able to take turns in conversation, sign spontaneously rather than as a response to drilling or coercion, and comment on interesting phenomena. Based on these stringent criteria, according to the critics, the apes do not appear to be really communicating.

The proponents of ape language counter that those who deny the validity of this research have never worked with these animals. Researchers who have a close working familiarity with the apes in question are convinced of the sophistication of the animals' communicative abilities. They claim evidence of gorillas using signs to show humor, to make insults, to threaten, to produce metaphorical language, and to engage in fantasy play. Finally, they point out that new fields of investigation always create controversy. They add that subhuman primates have not been taught to speak, however, because the outer layer of their brain hemispheres is not sufficiently refined.

One of the major hazards for deep-sea divers is decompression sickness (DCS), more commonly known as the "bends." This sometimes fatal condition is caused by gas bubbles forming in the bloodstream if a diver ascends too rapidly. These bubbles travel in the blood and may become lodged anyplace in the body. Most commonly, they get trapped in joints, particularly in the joints of the spine. The resulting pain causes the diver to bend over, hence the name of the condition.

The reason gas bubbles form has to do with the saturation and desaturation of body tissues with various gases. At increasingly great depths, the diver breathes air at higher pressures. This results in an increased quantity of air being dissolved in the bloodstream. Different body tissues are saturated with different gases from the air at different rates. When the diver rises to the surface, oxygen is used by the body tissues, carbon dioxide is released quickly, and nitrogen remains. The remaining nitrogen needs to be released gradually from the bloodstream and body tissues. |If the nitrogen is subjected to a too rapid pressure reduction, it forms bubbles. Not only do these bubbles collect in joints, but they also become trapped in capillaries. This entrapment prevents blood and oxygen from supplying necessary nutrients to body tissues, which consequently begin to die.

Saturation and desaturation are affected by various factors such as the depth of the water and the length of time and amount of exertion used while underwater. Other factors must also be taken into account when determining a safe ascent rate. These include the diver's sex and body build, the number of dives undertaken within the previous twelve hours, the time spent at the dive location before the dive, and the composition of the respiration gas.

Diving tables set guidelines based on statistical probabilities of getting the bends. However, someone who stays within the suggested limits can still get DCS. Since even a mild case can leave a diver permanently crippled, it is imperative that divers recognize the symptoms. Unfortunately, such symptoms can be similar to those of the flu or a strained muscle, something that occurs frequently when divers are handling heavy equipment, using improperly fitted gear, or engaging in unaccustomed activity. Because even professionals can have difficulty diagnosing DCS, the most reliable test is to recompress the patient and see whether the symptoms abate.

One type of structure that I would like to discuss is called a kiva. The kiva is considered to have had a mainly religious and ceremonial purpose. In this diagram, which shows the kind of kiva typical of the Mesa Verde area, you can see that the structure is circular in shape. Mesa Verde kivas usually have six stone pillars built into the wall. These pillars are called pilasters and were used to support the roof beams. The fire pit can be found in the center of the room. This short, low wall behind the fire pit served as a deflector for the air intake coming from behind it. Notice the small round hole in the floor. This is called a sipapu. The Anasazi people probably regarded it as a symbolic entrance to the underworld.

lectureGroups.transcript:
Although we learn to count from an early age, learning to count is quite complicated. First, children need to learn the names of the numbers in their particular language. They learn the numbers, but often get-+z"'ShowText$#uid#-26C{:'`modification-dateWed Jul 31 22:54:47 2002empts to mimic nature.
Researchers have investigated several interesting areas. For example, they have studied how the molecular structure of antler bone contributes to its amazing toughness, how the skin structure of a worm contributes to its ability to crawl, how the sea cucumber softens its skeleton and changes shape so that it can squeeze throughe order wrong. Eventually, with much parental correction, children learn the numbers up to twenty, but this does not indicate an ability to count.
The next step is learning that each number can represent or correspond to a real object. This notion takes time to perfect. If you watch young children trying to count a row of toys, you will notice that they begin well but after counting the first few toys, they say the number names without matching the number to a toy. Perfecting the ability to match a number to an object occurs later in the child's development.
The final stage in learning to count is achieved when the child learns that the number of the last object in the row describes the total number of objects in that row. In other words, if there is a row of twelve objects, the number twelve represents not the final object but the whole collection of objects, or group of twelve. This distinction is a significant step in the child's understanding of basic mathematics.

questions.feedback: Since learning to count is part of a child's development, this talk would probably be aimed at a group of people studying child development.

It's an interactive computer system that allows you to make critica'8s	/&>ëT6L39-44WOMAN 1: Today I want to cohealth-care decisions without endangering patients' lives. The system uses a computer with a touch screen and a videodisc, and it takes you step-by-step through simulated emergency situations. For instance, on the computer screen, you might see an elderly man being wheeled into the emergency room, complaining that he can't breathe. You listen to an account of his symptoms and then decide what to do. If you make the right decision, the computer answers, "Correct."
